The pilot reported that before the flight the 12-gallon fuselage fuel tank contained about 8.5 gallons of fuel and that the cork-and-wire fuel indicator gauge installed in the fuel tank cap was about 5.5 inches above an empty indication. The pilot noted that the airplane’s Continental C85 engine consumed 4.5 to 5 gallons per hour at a cruise power setting.

The pilot reported that at 1602 the local flight departed Pelican Rapids Municipal Airport (47Y), Pelican Rapids, Minnesota. The pilot flew a meandering route over the lakes in the Pelican Rapids area, then over Highway 34 west to Barnesville, Minnesota, then to the south before turning back toward 47Y.

The pilot reported that about 1 hour and 15 minutes had elapsed since departure when the airplane was on the left downwind for runway 33 at 47Y. The pilot acknowledged that the flight was 10 to 15 minutes longer than he had planned for, but the cork-and-wire fuel indicator gauge was about an inch above the empty indication. The pilot considered flying a circle-to-short final because there were no other aircraft in the traffic pattern; however, ultimately, he decided to fly a normal traffic pattern to runway 33.

The pilot reported he reduced engine throttle and the airplane entered a descent during the turn from downwind to base leg. The airplane’s altitude and airspeed were reportedly lower-than-normal after the turn to base leg. The pilot increased the engine throttle but there was no response from the engine. The pilot reported that the engine continued to operate at a near idle power setting and at no point sputtered or quit. The airplane continued to descend rapidly toward trees. The pilot does not recall the final sequence of events that led to the impact with terrain. The airplane sustained substantial damage to the forward fuselage during the nose-low impact into a soybean field.

On September 29, 2026, about 1828 central daylight time, a Cessna 152 II airplane, N69009, sustained substantial damage when it was involved in an accident near Bolingbrook, Illinois. The flight instructor and the student pilot sustained minor injuries. The airplane was operated as a Title 14 Code of Federal Regulations Part 91 instructional flight.
The purpose of the local area flight was for the flight instructor to provide instruction to the student pilot, as part of JWA Flight School. JWA Flight School is based at the Bolingbrook’s Clow International Airport (1C5), Bolingbrook, Illinois.
The airplane had a preflight inspection performed by both the flight instructor and the student pilot, and no abnormalities were noted. The student pilot was stationed in the left front seat, and the flight instructor was stationed in the right front seat. The airplane had about 24.5 gallons of 100 low lead fuel onboard for the flight.
The engine runup process was completed and no abnormalities were noted. During the initial climb from runway 18 at 1C5, the student pilot who was manipulating the flight controls noted that “something was not right.” The flight instructor then immediately assumed the flight controls. She observed the tachometer and noticed that the engine RPM had decreased to about 20 RPM. She then executed the emergency procedure checklist and realized the airplane did not have sufficient engine power to climb due to the partial power loss, and the airplane was losing altitude. She performed a forced landing to a flat grass sports field in a residential area, about 0.25 miles southwest of the departure end of runway 18.
The airplane came to rest upright in a nose-down profile on the grass field. During the impact sequence, the empennage separated about midspan. The student pilot was able to egress from the airplane on his own accord; however, the flight instructor was removed from the airplane by a bystander. The airplane sustained substantial damage to the fuselage, both wings, and the empennage. The airplane was recovered from the accident site and transported to a secure location for future examination.
The airplane was manufactured in 1978. The airplane was equipped with a Lycoming Engines O-235-L2C reciprocating engine and a McCauley Propeller 1A103/TCM6958 fixed-pitch two-blade aluminum propeller.
A review of the airplane’s maintenance records showed that an annual inspection was performed by a mechanic on July 23, 2026, for the airframe, the engine, and the propeller. Since the annual inspection occurred, the airplane had accumulated 40.9 hours. At the time of the accident, the airplane had accumulated a total of 14,851.9 hours.
The flight instructor completed a flight review on April 24, 2025.

On September 30, 2026, about 1410 central daylight time, a Cessna 525B, Dominican Republic registration HI1127, was substantially damaged when it was involved in an accident at Winston Field Airport (SNK), Snyder, Texas. The two pilots and one passenger were not injured. The airplane was operated by Panorama Jets as a Title 14 Code of Federal Regulations (CFR) Part 129 non-scheduled passenger flight.
The flight departed from McClellan Airfield (MCC), Sacramento, California, at 0924 Pacific daylight time, on an instrument flight rules flight plan and proceeded to SNK at a cruise altitude of flight level 410 (FL410). The cockpit voice recorder (CVR) revealed that during the approach to SNK, which is a non-towered airport, the pilots received the SNK automated weather information four times. The reported weather was visual meteorological conditions, and the wind was generally from the south-southwest about 13 knots, gusting to 19 knots. The pilots received an approach clearance from air traffic control, then canceled their IFR flight plan and switched to the SNK common traffic advisory frequency. ADS-B data showed that the airplane’s transponder code changed from the assigned IFR code to 1200 at 1406:40, when the airplane was about 8 nautical miles (nm) south of the runway 35 threshold.
The pilot-in-command (PIC), who was the pilot flying, reported that he selected runway 35 because it was the only runway with an instrument approach. Runway 17/35 is 5,599 ft long and 100 ft wide, with an asphalt surface.
The company’s dispatch paperwork, which the pilots were referencing, included a runway analysis prepared at 1821 CDT the evening before the flight. The analysis was computed for landing on runway 17 using a forecast wind from 205° at 12 knots. It indicated “landing impossible” on runway 35 with that wind condition.
ADS-B data showed that the airplane turned onto final approach for runway 35 at 1407, about 7 nm from the runway threshold. About 3 nm to the threshold, the airplane’s groundspeed was about 150 knots. The airplane crossed the runway 35 threshold at 1409:33 at a groundspeed of 149 knots, about 90 ft above the runway elevation. At 1409:40, the data indicated that the airplane was on the runway about 1,700 ft beyond the threshold, at a groundspeed of 138 knots. The groundspeed decreased to 80 knots at 1409:57, about 4,900 ft beyond the threshold, and then increased. The airplane passed the departure end of the runway at 1410:02 at a groundspeed of 92 knots, and it reached 104 knots about 400 ft beyond the runway end. Between 1410:07 and 1410:10, the groundspeed decreased from 104 to 54 knots, about 920 to 1,180 ft beyond the runway end. The final ADS-B position, at 1410:22, was about 1,415 ft beyond the departure end of runway 35 and about 60 ft left of the extended runway centerline.
